note: Evidence examples (9 -> 18): two per capability, one conceptual and one applied. Draft for review.

capabilities.statement: Explain how academic searching differs from everyday searching

evidence.title: Web and library search compared against the Seven Pillars
evidence.example: You run the same question twice, once on a general web search engine and once on the library search, and compare the first ten results. Using the SCONUL Seven Pillars of Information Literacy (SCONUL 2011), you note which pillars the academic search asked more of you, such as Scope and Evaluate, and explain the difference in a short paragraph (for example, an environmental science question on microplastics in rivers returning blogs on the web and peer-reviewed studies in the library).
evidence.artefact: A side-by-side table of the two result lists, with notes against the pillars and a 150-word explanation of the difference.
grounding: model: SCONUL Seven Pillars of Information Literacy (SCONUL 2011)

evidence.title: Leaflet sources sorted into everyday and academic finds
evidence.example: Volunteering at a youth club, you are asked to find information for a leaflet on vaping. You show the leader that a quick web search mostly returns adverts, news and opinion, while NHS guidance and research studies give sources you could cite and check. You explain in plain terms why the second kind of search is different and when each is good enough (for example, a forum post being fine for slang terms but not for health risks).
evidence.artefact: The draft leaflet with its source list split into everyday and academic finds, plus the youth leader's comment.
grounding: practice: youth club volunteering

genericOutcomes.title: Search results compared against a structured information-literacy model
genericOutcomes.example: You run the same question twice, once through a general web search engine and once through a scholarly search tool, then compare the first ten results from each. Using a structured information-literacy model, you note which stages the scholarly search demanded more of you, such as scoping terms carefully and evaluating sources, and explain the difference in a short paragraph.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A side-by-side table of the two result lists, with notes against the model's stages and a short written explanation.
grounding: model: SCONUL Seven Pillars of Information Literacy (SCONUL 2011)

genericOutcomes.title: Everyday finds and citable sources sorted for one task
genericOutcomes.example: You are asked to find information for a short piece of public-facing writing on a topic you do not know well. A quick web search mostly returns adverts, opinion and news, while a scholarly search turns up sources you could cite and check. You sort your finds into the two groups and explain in plain terms why the second kind of search is different, and when each kind is good enough for the job.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short source list split into everyday and citable finds, with a brief written explanation of the difference and when each is used.
grounding: professional: Distinguishes citable, checkable sources from general information before using them in written work.

genericOutcomes.title: Explanation of how structured searching differs from casual searching
genericOutcomes.example: You compare a casual search of the kind used to settle an everyday question with a structured search aimed at scholarly sources, and set out in your own words what changes: the terms you choose, the places you look, and the checks you apply before trusting a result. You explain why a structured search takes longer but produces material you can defend, using a recognised model of information literacy to frame the stages involved.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A written explanation, with a short diagram or list, of the stages that separate structured searching from casual searching.
grounding: model: SCONUL Seven Pillars of Information Literacy (SCONUL 2011)
benchmark: none (unattributed; written from capability statement)

genericOutcomes.title: Structured search explained to someone unfamiliar with it
genericOutcomes.example: Someone asks why you are taking longer over a search instead of just using a quick web search engine. You explain, in plain terms, that a structured search uses specific terms, trusted sources and a check on currency and authority, and that this is what separates it from an everyday search. You give one concrete example of a term you refined and why the refined version returned better material.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short written or spoken explanation of structured versus everyday searching, with one worked example of a refined search term.
grounding: professional: Explains the difference between a quick everyday search and a structured search to someone who has not done one before.
benchmark: none (unattributed; written from capability statement)

capabilities.statement: Use the library discovery service to locate scholarly sources

evidence.title: Discovery service search diary mapped to Kuhlthau's six stages
evidence.example: You use the library discovery service for a first assignment and keep a short diary under Kuhlthau's (1991) six stages: initiation, selection, exploration, formulation, collection and presentation. You record what you searched, what you found and how you felt at each stage, including the uncertainty Kuhlthau describes during exploration (for example, a first-year business student searching for sources on the gig economy who feels lost until a narrower focus on delivery riders forms).
evidence.artefact: A one-page search diary with stage headings, screenshots of discovery service results and a list of five scholarly sources located.
grounding: ing:doc:information-search-process-kuhlthau-1991

evidence.title: Placement search on a firm's subscription legal database
evidence.example: On a work placement at a solicitors' firm, you are asked to find recent commentary on a change to tenancy law. You use the firm's subscription database the way you learned to use the library discovery service: a subject search, filters for practitioner and academic journals, and a check of full-text access. This shows you can locate reliable sources quickly with an organisation's own systems (for example, finding two journal commentaries and the relevant statute in one session).
evidence.artefact: A short search record listing the database, the filters applied and the sources found, initialled by your placement supervisor.
grounding: professional: Finds reliable information quickly with an organisation's knowledge systems and subscription services.
professional: SCONUL Seven Pillars: Gather

genericOutcomes.title: Search diary mapped to the six stages of the search process
genericOutcomes.example: You use a scholarly discovery search tool for a piece of work and keep a short diary structured around six stages: initiation, selection, exploration, formulation, collection and presentation. At each stage you record what you searched, what you found and how you felt, including the uncertainty that typically appears during exploration before a narrower focus forms and searching becomes easier.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A one-page search diary with the six stages as headings, screenshots of results and a list of five scholarly sources found.
grounding: ing:doc:information-search-process-kuhlthau-1991

genericOutcomes.title: Subscription database search carried out using discovery-service skills
genericOutcomes.example: You are asked to find recent, reliable material on a specific question using an organisation's own subscription database rather than the library discovery service you learned on. You apply the same approach: a subject search, filters narrowing results to serious published sources, and a check that you can access the full text, so you can show you locate reliable information quickly with whatever system is in front of you.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short search record listing the database used, the filters applied and the sources found in one session.
grounding: professional: Finds reliable information quickly with an organisation's knowledge systems and subscription services.
framework: SCONUL Seven Pillars: Gather

genericOutcomes.title: Scholarly sources located and selected as appropriate to a question
genericOutcomes.example: Given an unfamiliar question, you use a dedicated search tool rather than a general one, choosing terms and filters that narrow results to material suited to the question's level and subject matter. You explain, stage by stage, how your search moved from a broad starting point towards sources you judged appropriate, drawing on an established model of how people search when they do not yet know exactly what they need.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A written account of the search, its stages and the final list of sources judged appropriate to the question.
grounding: ing:doc:information-search-process-kuhlthau-1991
benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/information-and-sources

genericOutcomes.title: Appropriate sources located quickly using a dedicated search system
genericOutcomes.example: Asked to find material to support a decision, you go straight to a dedicated search system rather than a general web search, choosing filters and terms that match the kind of source the question needs. You locate several appropriate items within a working session and note briefly why each one fits, so someone checking your work can see the selection was not accidental.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short list of sources found through a dedicated search system, each with a one-line note on why it fits.
grounding: professional: Finds reliable information quickly with an organisation's knowledge systems and subscription services.
benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/information-and-sources

capabilities.statement: Follow a staged search, starting from the reading list and what one already knows

evidence.title: Staged search plan starting from prior knowledge and reading list
evidence.example: Before searching, you write down what you already know about the topic and pick the two most useful items from your reading list. You then follow a staged search: the reading list, the references in those items, then the discovery service. You link each stage to Kuhlthau's (1991) model, showing how prior knowledge helps you move from initiation to selection (for example, a psychology student starting an essay on eyewitness memory from a set textbook chapter).
evidence.artefact: A staged search plan with a 'what I already know' box, reading list items, followed-up references and new sources, each stage labelled.
grounding: ing:doc:information-search-process-kuhlthau-1991

evidence.title: Teaching assistant search starting from what the school holds
evidence.example: Working as a teaching assistant, you are asked to gather ideas for a reading intervention. You start with what the school already holds, such as past plans, staff knowledge and a training handout, then follow up the sources those cite before searching further. This shows a staged search that begins from existing knowledge (for example, finding that a colleague trialled paired reading last year, which narrows what you need to look for).
evidence.artefact: A short summary of what the school already held, the sources you followed up and the gap your new search filled.
grounding: professional: Starts a search from what the organisation and its people already hold before looking further.
professional: SCONUL Seven Pillars: Identify, Scope

genericOutcomes.title: Staged search plan built from prior knowledge and a set reading list
genericOutcomes.example: Before searching further, you write down what you already know about a topic and pick the two most useful items from a set reading list. You then follow a staged search: the reading list first, the references those items cite next, and a wider search tool last. You link each stage to a recognised model of the search process, showing how starting from prior knowledge moves you from an uncertain first stage towards a workable focus.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A staged search plan with a what-I-already-know section, reading list items, followed-up references and new sources, labelled by stage.
grounding: ing:doc:information-search-process-kuhlthau-1991

genericOutcomes.title: Staged search starting from what a team already holds
genericOutcomes.example: Asked to gather ideas on a topic for a piece of work, you start with what your own team or organisation already holds, such as past documents, a colleague's experience and an existing handout, then follow up the sources those materials cite before searching more widely. This shows a staged search beginning from existing knowledge rather than an open search from nothing, and narrows what you still need to find.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short summary of what was already held, the sources followed up from it, and the gap the new search filled.
grounding: professional: Starts a search from what the organisation and its people already hold before looking further.
framework: SCONUL Seven Pillars: Identify, Scope

genericOutcomes.title: Independent search sequence planned before asking for help
genericOutcomes.example: Given a new topic, you set out, before doing anything else, what you already know, which sources you intend to check first and in what order, and only ask for help once that sequence runs out. You keep a short record showing the stages you worked through on your own, which demonstrates that you can manage a piece of your own learning independently rather than waiting to be directed through every step.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A written search sequence with its stages, plus a note on which stage you reached unaided before asking for help.
grounding: ing:doc:information-search-process-kuhlthau-1991
benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/independent-and-self-directed-learning

genericOutcomes.title: Independent search carried out before raising a question with others
genericOutcomes.example: Given an open task, you check what is already available to you, follow up the sources that material points to, and only raise a question with someone else once those avenues are exhausted. You keep a brief note of what you checked and in what order, which shows you can work and manage your own search independently rather than relying on direction at every stage.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A brief note listing the sources checked in order and the point at which you raised a question with someone else.
grounding: professional: Starts a search from what the organisation and its people already hold before looking further.
benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/independent-and-self-directed-learning

capabilities.statement: Identify keywords and synonyms from the task

evidence.title: PICO concept grid with keywords and synonyms
evidence.example: You break an assignment question into concepts using the PICO framework (Richardson et al. 1995): population, intervention, comparison and outcome. For each concept you list keywords, synonyms, spelling variants and related terms, and explain why you kept or dropped each one. This shows you can turn a task into searchable language (for example, in physiotherapy, 'older adults', 'elderly' and 'aged 65 and over' as population terms for a question on balance training and falls).
evidence.artefact: A concept grid under the four PICO headings, with keyword and synonym lists and notes on the terms you rejected.
grounding: model: PICO framework for clinical questions (Richardson et al. 1995)

evidence.title: Keyword list built from a brief and customer language
evidence.example: On a marketing internship, you are asked to find what customers and trade press say about a product. You pull keywords from the brief, then add the words customers actually use in reviews and social posts, and test which terms find useful material. This shows you can identify keywords and synonyms from a real task (for example, 'sustainable', 'eco-friendly', 'green' and 'refill' for a refillable cleaning product).
evidence.artefact: A keyword and synonym list drawn from the brief and customer language, with a note on which terms found the most useful results.
grounding: practice: marketing internship

genericOutcomes.title: Concept grid breaking a task into keywords and synonyms
genericOutcomes.example: You break a task's question down into its separate concepts using a structured framework for turning questions into searchable terms. For each concept you list keywords, synonyms, spelling variants and related terms, and explain why you kept or dropped each one. This shows you can turn an ordinary task description into language a search tool can actually use.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A concept grid with headings for each part of the question, keyword and synonym lists, and notes on rejected terms.
grounding: model: PICO framework for structuring questions (Richardson et al. 1995)

genericOutcomes.title: Keyword list built from a brief and everyday language
genericOutcomes.example: Given a short brief, you pull out the obvious keywords it uses, then add the words people actually use when talking about the same topic in everyday language, such as reviews or informal posts. You test which of these terms actually finds useful material and which return mostly noise. This shows you can identify keywords and synonyms from a real task rather than relying on the brief's exact wording.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A keyword and synonym list drawn from a brief and everyday language, with a note on which terms worked best.
grounding: professional: Builds a keyword list from a brief plus the language people actually use about a topic.

genericOutcomes.title: Keywords and synonyms identified before a search begins
genericOutcomes.example: Given a task description, you identify the separate ideas within it, then generate keywords, synonyms and alternative spellings for each one before running a single search. You justify which terms you expect to be most productive and which you expect to narrow results too far, showing that identifying search language is a distinct step that happens before searching rather than something worked out by trial and error alone.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A written list of task concepts with keywords and synonyms for each, and a short justification of the choices made.
grounding: model: PICO framework for structuring questions (Richardson et al. 1995)
benchmark: none (unattributed; written from capability statement)

genericOutcomes.title: Search terms built from a task's own wording and common usage
genericOutcomes.example: Given a short task, you list the exact words it uses, then add synonyms, abbreviations and the terms other people commonly use for the same idea, so a search is not limited to one way of phrasing the question. You note which added term made the biggest difference to the results, giving a concrete reason for widening your search language beyond the task's original wording.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short list of original and added search terms, with a note on which addition improved the results most.
grounding: professional: Builds a keyword list from a brief plus the language people actually use about a topic.
benchmark: none (unattributed; written from capability statement)

capabilities.statement: Plan a search strategy with keywords and Boolean operators

evidence.title: Boolean search strategy placed at Kuhlthau's formulation stage
evidence.example: You write a search strategy that combines concepts with AND, synonyms with OR and excludes noise with NOT, adding truncation and limiters such as date range. Drawing on Kuhlthau (1991), you place the plan at the formulation stage, where a focused perspective lets you search with purpose, and explain how the strings reflect that focus (for example, in criminology: ('knife crime' OR 'weapon carrying') AND (youth OR adolescen*) AND prevention).
evidence.artefact: A written search strategy with search strings, limiters and reasons for each choice, plus a screenshot of results from one database.
grounding: ing:doc:information-search-process-kuhlthau-1991

evidence.title: Documented prior-art search for a product design live brief
evidence.example: On a product design live brief, you plan and document a prior-art search on a patent database before your team develops a new folding bike lock. You set out the keywords, Boolean strings and classification codes, then record dates and hit counts so someone else could rerun the search. This shows a planned, reproducible strategy for a real decision (for example, finding an expired patent that frees your team to use a hinge design).
evidence.artefact: A documented search log with strings, databases, dates and hit counts, shared with the client or module tutor.
grounding: professional: Plans and documents searches for evidence, policy, competitors or prior art.
professional: SCONUL Seven Pillars: Plan

genericOutcomes.title: Boolean search strategy placed within the search process
genericOutcomes.example: You write a search strategy that combines concepts with AND, synonyms with OR, and excludes unwanted terms with NOT, adding truncation and limiters such as a date range. You place this plan within an established stage of the search process, where having a focused perspective lets you search with real purpose, and explain how your search strings reflect that focus rather than being guesswork.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A written search strategy with search strings, limiters and reasons for each choice, plus a results screenshot.
grounding: ing:doc:information-search-process-kuhlthau-1991

genericOutcomes.title: Documented search strategy for a real decision
genericOutcomes.example: Before a team moves ahead with a plan, you plan and document a search on a specialised database to check whether something similar already exists. You set out the keywords, Boolean strings and category codes used, then record dates and result counts so someone else could rerun the same search later. This shows a planned, reproducible strategy that supports a real decision rather than an informal look.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A documented search log with strings, databases, dates and result counts, shared with whoever needs to see it.
grounding: professional: Plans and documents searches for evidence, policy, competitors or prior art.
framework: SCONUL Seven Pillars: Plan

genericOutcomes.title: Search strings built and explained using Boolean logic
genericOutcomes.example: Given a topic with several components, you build search strings that combine the components with AND, bring in alternative wordings with OR, and remove unwanted meanings with NOT, adding truncation where a word has several endings. You explain each choice in terms of a recognised stage of the search process, where a settled focus allows precise, purposeful searching rather than a broad, unfocused look.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A set of Boolean search strings with a short written explanation of the reasoning behind each operator used.
grounding: ing:doc:information-search-process-kuhlthau-1991
benchmark: none (unattributed; written from capability statement)

genericOutcomes.title: Reproducible search strategy planned and recorded for others
genericOutcomes.example: Before searching, you plan a strategy using keywords and Boolean operators, then record every string, filter and date used so that someone else could rerun the exact same search and get the same results. You note the result count at each stage and briefly explain why you added or removed a term, turning what could be an informal look into a planned, reproducible piece of work.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A search log recording each string, filter, date and result count, written so another person could repeat it.
grounding: professional: Plans and documents searches for evidence, policy, competitors or prior art.
benchmark: none (unattributed; written from capability statement)

capabilities.statement: Refine a search in cycles, reflecting on the results each time

evidence.title: Three-round search reflection using Bates' berrypicking model
evidence.example: You run a search in at least three rounds, and after each round you record what the results showed and what you changed. You use Bates' (1989) berrypicking model to explain why your query evolved as you read, rather than staying fixed, and judge whether each change helped. This shows you refine a search through reflection (for example, a music education search moving from music and wellbeing to group singing with older adults after early results pointed to choirs).
evidence.artefact: A three-round search reflection showing each query, a sample of results, what you learned and the change you made.
grounding: model: Berrypicking model of information seeking (Bates 1989)

evidence.title: Weekly search cycles as a student research assistant
evidence.example: As a paid student research assistant on a sociology project about remote working, you run weekly searches for the team. Each week you review the results with the lead researcher, note what was missing, and refine your terms and databases for the next cycle. This shows you reflect on results and adjust in a real project (for example, adding 'hybrid working' after the first cycle missed most studies published since 2020).
evidence.artefact: A shared search log or weekly update emails showing each cycle's query, results and the lead researcher's feedback.
grounding: practice: student research assistant role

genericOutcomes.title: Search refined across rounds using a model of evolving queries
genericOutcomes.example: You run a search in at least three rounds, and after each one you record what the results showed and what you changed as a result. You draw on a recognised model of information seeking, which describes a search query evolving as you read rather than staying fixed from the start, and you judge for each round whether the change you made actually helped.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A three-round search reflection showing each query used, a sample of results and the change made after each round.
grounding: model: Berrypicking model of information seeking (Bates 1989)

genericOutcomes.title: Search cycles refined with regular review from a colleague
genericOutcomes.example: Supporting a piece of ongoing work, you run searches on a regular cycle, such as weekly, and review the results each time with someone else involved in the work. Each review identifies what was missing from the previous round, and you adjust your terms or the places you search for the next cycle. This shows reflection on results and real adjustment, rather than repeating the same search unchanged.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A shared search log or update notes showing each cycle's query, results and the feedback that shaped the next one.
grounding: professional: Reviews search results with someone else involved in the work and adjusts terms for the next cycle.

genericOutcomes.title: Search cycles judged and adjusted through reflection
genericOutcomes.example: You treat a search as a sequence of rounds rather than one attempt, and after each round you judge explicitly what worked, what returned too much noise and what the results suggest you should try next. You keep a short note after each round stating the change you are making and the reason for it, so that the refinement can be traced rather than appearing as an unexplained shift in approach.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A round-by-round record stating what each search returned, the judgement made and the change carried forward.
grounding: model: Berrypicking model of information seeking (Bates 1989)
benchmark: none (unattributed; written from capability statement)

genericOutcomes.title: Search terms adjusted each cycle based on a stated reason
genericOutcomes.example: Running searches to support an ongoing piece of work, you treat each attempt as one cycle in a sequence rather than a final answer. After every cycle you state in writing what the results were missing, change your terms or sources accordingly, and carry that reasoning into the next cycle. This shows a search that improves through reflection rather than one that stays the same no matter what the results show.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A log of search cycles, each with the stated gap identified and the specific change carried into the next cycle.
grounding: professional: Reviews search results with someone else involved in the work and adjusts terms for the next cycle.
benchmark: none (unattributed; written from capability statement)

capabilities.statement: Extend a search by citation searching, databases and Google Scholar

evidence.title: Citation map from one seed paper, backward and forward
evidence.example: Starting from one key paper, you search backwards through its reference list and forwards through 'cited by' in Google Scholar and a subject database, recording what each route added. You frame this with Kuhlthau's (1991) collection stage, when a clear focus lets you gather comprehensively, and explain why citation searching suited that point in your search (for example, in chemistry, tracing a landmark paper on a catalyst forward to its recent applications).
evidence.artefact: A citation map showing the seed paper with backward and forward links, and a table of new sources each tool found.
grounding: ing:doc:information-search-process-kuhlthau-1991

evidence.title: Ward evidence summary extended beyond the first database
evidence.example: On a nursing placement, the ward manager asks for evidence on pressure ulcer prevention. After searching one database, you extend the search with a second database, forward citation searching and national guidance, and note what each added. This shows you can search beyond the first tool so the evidence is properly covered (for example, finding a recent Cochrane review only by following citations forward from an older trial).
evidence.artefact: An evidence summary for the ward with a record of the tools used and what each added, signed by your practice supervisor.
grounding: professional: Searches beyond the first tool to cover the evidence comprehensively.
professional: SCONUL Seven Pillars: Scope, Gather

genericOutcomes.title: Citation map extended backward and forward from one source
genericOutcomes.example: Starting from one key source, you search backwards through its reference list and forwards through citation-tracking tools to see what later work builds on it, recording what each route adds that the other misses. You frame this using a stage of the search process where having a clear focus lets you gather material comprehensively, and explain why citation searching suited that particular point in your work.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A citation map showing the seed source with backward and forward links, and a table of what each route added.
grounding: ing:doc:information-search-process-kuhlthau-1991

genericOutcomes.title: Evidence search extended beyond a single tool for full coverage
genericOutcomes.example: Asked for current evidence on a specific question, you search one database first, then extend the search with a second database, forward citation tracking and relevant published guidance, noting what each addition contributed. This shows you can search beyond the first tool so the final evidence picture is properly covered rather than resting on whatever the first search happened to surface.
genericOutcomes.artefact: An evidence summary recording the tools used in sequence and what each one added that the previous tool missed.
grounding: professional: Searches beyond the first tool to cover the evidence comprehensively.
framework: SCONUL Seven Pillars: Scope, Gather

genericOutcomes.title: Comprehensive source coverage built through citation tracking
genericOutcomes.example: Rather than treating one database as the end of a search, you follow a key source both backwards through what it cites and forwards through what later cites it, then cross-check the result against a second search tool. You select only the sources that are genuinely appropriate to the question at hand, discarding material a tool returns that does not actually fit, and explain your selection in each case.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A written account of backward and forward citation tracking, with the final selected sources and reasons for inclusion.
grounding: ing:doc:information-search-process-kuhlthau-1991
benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/information-and-sources

genericOutcomes.title: Sources selected as appropriate after a search extended across tools
genericOutcomes.example: Given a question that needs solid evidence behind it, you run an initial search, then extend it with citation tracking and at least one further tool, and from everything found you select only the sources genuinely appropriate to the question, setting aside the rest with a brief reason. This shows a search that goes beyond a single tool and ends in a deliberately selected, appropriate set of sources.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short record of the tools used, the sources selected as appropriate and the reasons given for excluding others.
grounding: professional: Searches beyond the first tool to cover the evidence comprehensively.
benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/information-and-sources

capabilities.statement: Evaluate sources for currency, authority and relevance to own knowledge

evidence.title: Source evaluation matrix tracking changing relevance judgements
evidence.example: You evaluate eight sources for a dissertation proposal against currency, authority and relevance, adding a column on how each relates to what you already know. Using Kuhlthau's (1991) stages, you note how your judgements of relevance changed between exploration and formulation, and why you kept or dropped sources (for example, in architecture, keeping an older daylight study because later work still builds on it).
evidence.artefact: An evaluation matrix of eight sources scored for currency, authority and relevance, with notes on how your judgements changed over time.
grounding: ing:doc:information-search-process-kuhlthau-1991

evidence.title: Source checks before publishing a student newspaper story
evidence.example: As an editor on the student newspaper, you check every source in a story on rising rents before it is published. You judge each for currency, authority and relevance to the claim it supports, and decide which can carry the story and which need replacing. This shows you can judge whether information is reliable enough to act on (for example, replacing a 2019 letting agency survey with current official rental price data).
evidence.artefact: A source-checking sheet for one published article with your verdict on each source, alongside the final published piece.
grounding: professional: Judges whether information is reliable and relevant enough to base a decision on.
professional: ACRL Framework: Authority Is Constructed and Contextual

genericOutcomes.title: Evaluation matrix tracking how relevance judgements change
genericOutcomes.example: You evaluate a set of sources for a substantial piece of work against currency, authority and relevance, adding a column on how each one relates to what you already know. Using a recognised model of how a search develops over time, you note how your judgement of a source's relevance shifted as your own understanding grew, and explain why you kept some older sources and dropped some newer ones.
genericOutcomes.artefact: An evaluation matrix scoring each source for currency, authority and relevance, with notes on judgements that changed.
grounding: ing:doc:information-search-process-kuhlthau-1991

genericOutcomes.title: Source checks completed before a piece goes public
genericOutcomes.example: Before a piece of writing is published, you check every source behind its claims, judging each for currency, authority and relevance to the specific claim it supports. You decide which sources can carry the piece as it stands and which need replacing, and you make at least one change, such as swapping an outdated figure for a current one. This shows reliability judgements made under a real deadline.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A source-checking sheet for one piece with a verdict on each source, alongside the version that was published.
grounding: professional: Judges whether information is reliable and relevant enough to base a decision on.
framework: ACRL Framework: Authority Is Constructed and Contextual

genericOutcomes.title: Reasoned judgement reached on a source's currency and authority
genericOutcomes.example: Given a source you are unsure whether to trust, you set out its currency, its authority and its relevance to what you already know, weigh these three against each other, and state a reasoned judgement on whether to use it. You show your reasoning clearly enough that someone else could check it and reach their own view, rather than simply stating a verdict without explaining how you got there.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short written judgement on one source covering currency, authority and relevance, with the reasoning set out.
grounding: ing:doc:information-search-process-kuhlthau-1991
benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/critical-evaluation-of-evidence-and-arguments

genericOutcomes.title: Reasoned decision made on which sources to rely on
genericOutcomes.example: Given several sources that disagree with each other, you weigh each one for currency, authority and relevance to the decision at hand, then reach a reasoned judgement on which to rely on and which to set aside. You state your reasoning in a way that someone checking your decision afterwards could follow and test, rather than leaving the choice unexplained.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short written decision naming the sources relied on, those set aside and the reasoning behind the choice.
grounding: professional: Judges whether information is reliable and relevant enough to base a decision on.
benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/critical-evaluation-of-evidence-and-arguments

capabilities.statement: Search comprehensively, judging when the discourse is covered

evidence.title: PRISMA-reported literature search with a justified end point
evidence.example: For a dissertation literature review, you run a documented search across several databases and report it with a PRISMA 2020 flow diagram (Page et al. 2021). You then set out when and why you judged the discourse covered, such as new searches returning only studies you already had and key reference lists adding nothing new (for example, in a pharmacy review of deprescribing in care homes).
evidence.artefact: A PRISMA flow diagram, the full search strings for each database and a 300-word statement justifying where your search stopped.
grounding: model: PRISMA 2020 reporting guideline (Page et al. 2021)

evidence.title: Evidence scan with an agreed stopping rule for a transport authority
evidence.example: On a placement with a regional transport authority, you lead an evidence scan on e-scooter safety to inform a policy decision. You search academic and grey literature, agree a stopping rule with your manager in advance, and report what the scan covers and what it may have missed. This shows independent judgement about when coverage is enough (for example, noting that most studies came from cities with very different road layouts).
evidence.artefact: The evidence scan report with its coverage and limitations section, and an email from your manager agreeing the stopping rule.
grounding: practice: placement with a regional transport authority

genericOutcomes.title: Literature search reported with a justified stopping point
genericOutcomes.example: For a substantial piece of work, you run a documented search across several sources and report it using a recognised reporting standard that tracks how many results came from where and what was excluded. You then set out, in writing, when and why you judged the material covered, such as new searches returning only items you already had, or key reference lists adding nothing further.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A reporting diagram, the full search details for each source used, and a short statement justifying where the search stopped.
grounding: model: PRISMA 2020 reporting guideline (Page et al. 2021)

genericOutcomes.title: Evidence scan completed against an agreed stopping rule
genericOutcomes.example: Asked to gather evidence to inform a decision, you agree in advance, with whoever needs the result, a rule for when the scan is complete, then search academic and other published material and report what the scan covers and what it may have missed. This shows a judgement about sufficient coverage that is made deliberately and agreed beforehand, rather than being decided by running out of time.
genericOutcomes.artefact: An evidence scan report with its coverage and limitations stated, and a note confirming the stopping rule was agreed.
grounding: professional: Agrees a stopping rule for an evidence scan in advance and reports what the search may have missed.

genericOutcomes.title: Reasoned judgement reached on when a search is sufficiently complete
genericOutcomes.example: Rather than stopping a search when you run out of time, you set out the evidence for treating the discourse as covered, such as further searches returning only sources you already hold, or reference lists adding nothing new. You weigh this evidence and reach a stated judgement on completeness, explaining your reasoning so someone else could check whether the search really was comprehensive.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A written statement of the evidence for completeness, the judgement reached and the reasoning behind it.
grounding: model: PRISMA 2020 reporting guideline (Page et al. 2021)
benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/critical-evaluation-of-evidence-and-arguments

genericOutcomes.title: Judgement made on when evidence-gathering is complete enough
genericOutcomes.example: Given a task that depends on gathering evidence, you weigh indicators such as repeated results, exhausted reference trails and diminishing new material, and reach a stated judgement on when to stop rather than continuing indefinitely or stopping arbitrarily. You record the reasoning behind that judgement so someone relying on your evidence can see it was a deliberate decision, not a default caused by running out of time.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short written judgement stating when the evidence-gathering stopped, the indicators used and the reasoning given.
grounding: professional: Agrees a stopping rule for an evidence scan in advance and reports what the search may have missed.
benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/critical-evaluation-of-evidence-and-arguments
